items.title: Trump vows 'tremendous tax' on companies building data centres abroad
paras: Donald Trump says he will tax US companies that build data centres overseas. ( Reuters: Carlos Barria )
US President Donald Trump has vowed to tax American companies that build data centres abroad.
US tech giants have recently committed billions of dollars to build data centres in Australia.
The president says the move is intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with China.
US President Donald Trump has vowed to impose a "tremendous tax" on American companies that build data centres abroad.
"We're not allowing data centres to go into other countries," he said in a White House news briefing.
The announcement could have significant implications in Australia, where US tech giants have already committed billions of dollars to build new data centres.
Microsoft announced a $25 billion investment in April to build data centre infrastructure key to operating artificial intelligence.
Australia has drawn growing interest from US tech firms due to its location, access to renewable energy and relative political stability.
But it is becoming an increasingly unpopular topic as anti-data centre sentiment spreads throughout the country.
Microsoft has announced a $25 billion investment to build data centre infrastructure key to operating artificial intelligence in Australia. ( Supplied: Jop van Hattum )
Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the electricity demands, utility costs, water usage and other local impacts data facilities can cause.
Opposition to data centres became a central issue in the US midterm elections as Republicans lost their majority in both the House and Senate of Congress.
Recent YouGov polling found nearly two-thirds of Americans were opposed to data centre construction in their community.
Despite voter anger, Donald Trump has remained a staunch advocate for them .
The facilities are critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI build-out.
The president said the move was intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with China.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centres because we're not going to let China [win], we're leading China," he said.
He did not provide further details about the proposed tax and admitted he had not yet told his own officials about the plan.
The Australian departments of Treasury and Industry, Science and Resources have been contacted for comment.

items.title: Australia strikes deal on AI talks with China
paras: Anthony Albanese says Australia has reached an agreement with China to hold talks and find new ways to work together on AI. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )
Australia and China have agreed to hold talks on artificial intelligence.
Australia has also signed a technology declaration with the US aimed at protecting the AI supply chain from China's interference.
Anthony Albanese is returning to Australia after 11 days at global summits.
Australia and China will hold talks on artificial intelligence as the two countries look for new ways to work together on the rapidly developing technology.

The agreement was reached during a meeting between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing overnight on Friday, where the leaders also discussed trade, climate change, health and tourism.

Mr Albanese spent about six hours in the Chinese capital for high-level talks, having met President Xi Jinping earlier that morning in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Anthony Albanese met Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )
At that meeting Mr Xi declared there had been a "complete turnaround" in China's relations with Australia despite the two countries' ongoing "differences".
Mr Albanese is due to return to Australia on Saturday after 11 days of international travel for the COP31 UN climate talks, ASEAN summit in Manila and APEC in China.
Anthony Albanese has held meetings with several world leaders on his 11-day trip, including Donald Trump and Andy Burnham. ( Ryohei Moriya/The Yomiuri Shimbun via AFP )

During the trip, Australia signed a new defence cooperation with the Philippines and Mr Albanese took part in meetings with several world leaders including US President Donald Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Mr Albanese also used his APEC speech to directly tell Russian President Vladimir Putin to end his illegal invasion of Ukraine "now".
"I have a responsibility to put Australia's position clearly and directly, and that is what I did," the prime minister said.
The new AI dialogue with China would allow the two governments to share their experiences of the technology as governments grapple with how it should be regulated.
Attendees ahead of the business round table in Beijing. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )
Speaking at a business round table in Beijing, Mr Albanese said AI had the potential to transform productivity and living standards.
The agreement to hold an AI dialogue comes just days after Australia signed a separate declaration with the United States partly designed to reduce reliance on China for critical technologies.

The US deal committed members to identifying vulnerable supply chains, protecting sensitive technology from theft or foreign interference, and reducing dependence on countries that could disrupt access to the infrastructure needed for AI.
Australian and Chinese leaders attended the ninth Australia-China CEO Roundtable, along with senior executives from some of the countries' biggest businesses. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )
During their formal annual meeting, Mr Li told Mr Albanese the improvement in relations between Australia and China had taken considerable work.
He said closer ties had delivered benefits to people in both countries and argued a stable relationship was particularly important given international tensions.
"Facts have shown that a more mature, stable and productive China–Australia relationship will only benefit the two countries, but also the region and beyond," he said.
Mr Albanese acknowledged the trust he had developed with Mr Li through their repeated meetings, saying the pair were now able to speak directly by phone when issues arose.
He also said the countries had shown they could manage disagreements while continuing to work together.

Mr Albanese said they could demonstrate to the region "that there can be different political systems, differences that can be negotiated wisely, but all in the spirit of recognising that working together is very much in our interests".
Mr Albanese and Mr Li also attended the ninth Australia–China CEO Roundtable, which brought together senior executives from some of the countries' biggest businesses.

items.title: Hiring freeze, graduate cuts and offshoring: How AI is hitting the jobs market
paras: Advertisement Business Workplace Employment Hiring freeze, graduate cuts and offshoring: How AI is hitting the jobs market Millie Muroi November 21, 2026 — 5:00am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A Despite the labour market taking a turn with several Australian industry giants revealing thousands of job cuts within weeks or days of each other and unemployment figures hitting a five-year-high, economists say it’s not all because of AI.

On Thursday, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed unemployment reached 4.9 per cent in October, the highest in five years. This month, KPMG announced it would cut 230 jobs and about 20 partners, Bunnings said it would slash 350 local jobs , and David Jones revealed it would axe 1500 jobs by the end of this year.

While AI may not be causing mass job losses, some economists say it is dampening business’ hiring intentions. Getty Images While National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Irvine has denied that AI is driving the bank’s latest round of 2500 redundancies , some firms such as Qantas, which announced it would cut 850 positions under a deal with AI services provider Accenture, have suggested the technology – and the efficiencies it brings – is a key reason for trimming their workforces.
So, how much of the recent job cuts are a result of AI uptake by firms, is there likely to be more disruption to come, and what might the employment landscape look like over coming years?
While AI has played a part in some of the recent wave of redundancies and retrenchments, economists say it’s not the only reason that unemployment has ticked up.

Bob Breunig, director of the Tax and Transfer Policy Institute at the Australian National University, says interest rates, which hit 4.85 per cent – the highest level since the global financial crisis – after the Reserve Bank lifted them for the fifth time this year, are one key factor.
“Interest rates are really starting to bite,” he says. “People pull back spending meaning retail has been hit, and some job losses are attributable to that.”
Major retailers such as David Jones, for example, have been squeezed by mounting debt and a slowdown in household spending.
Melbourne University labour economist Jeff Borland says while interest rates have played a major role, AI has also led to some job cuts.

“There have definitely been some retrenchments to do with AI,” he says, noting it is “very believable” for companies such as Canva – which earlier this month announced more than 1200 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles – to have been disrupted by AI given software designers are among the most exposed to the technology.
However, Borland also notes that some companies are likely dressing up job losses to avoid stronger backlash for offshoring.
“Historically, it’s often convenient for businesses to make job cuts and say it’s because of new technology coming along rather than saying they are offshoring jobs because that’s cheaper,” he says.

Australia Institute co-chief executive Richard Denniss also says one of the major drivers of recent job losses has been the Reserve Bank’s continued interest rates rises, which are aimed at dampening inflation but have also slowed the economy.
However, Denniss says some business leaders are likely packaging up job losses as a response to AI even when it is not the primary reason for their job cuts.

“Two things are happening at the same time: old-fashioned offshoring in pursuit of lower wages and reducing costs, and the need to convince investors that the company is preparing for AI,” he says. “Chief executives, such as at WiseTech and Telstra, are deliberately trying to signal they are forward-looking and gearing up for an AI revolution. They have to tell a story that they will not be eaten or threatened by AI, but enhanced by it.”
Evidence of mass job losses has not yet emerged in Australia, but there are signs of a hiring slowdown, especially in some occupations and programs.
Borland says looking at countries such as the US suggests there may be more disruption and job losses to come from AI uptake.
“We might not be able to predict the exact extent or timing, but the US, which is ahead of us, can give us an indication.”
In the US, there has been more noticeable evidence of job losses and slower employment growth tied to AI adoption, including a reduction in some entry-level jobs.
Breunig says the main immediate effect of AI on the jobs market is slower growth in employment rather than widespread job losses.

“We’re not yet seeing a lot of firing because of AI, but we are seeing downward revision in hiring because of AI,” he said, noting some big banks and consultancy firms he has spoken to have cut down their graduate intakes, specifically citing AI.
Denniss does not have a prediction for the extent of job losses from AI uptake, but believes the Reserve Bank is “massively underestimating” the effect of AI on the labour market.

“The only reason Anthropic and Open AI can be worth a trillion dollars is if businesses and government departments replace millions of workers with AI, swapping their wage bill for an AI bill,” he says. “Mass unemployment is not an unintended consequence of the AI boom, it’s the business plan [for AI companies]. Either companies such as Anthropic are not worth as much as markets think, or there are a hell of a lot of job losses to come.”
Although AI has led to some job losses, like most technologies, it is likely to create demand for new jobs and change the nature of the work we do.
“It could go either way,” Bruenig says. “Every time new technology is introduced, old jobs die and new jobs emerge, but it’s really hard to predict what those new jobs will look like.”

Breunig also says it may affect some intakes such as graduate programs more than others, and that it could change how jobs are done or the skills – such as softer human skills – that are sought after.

Borland says while some jobs such as computer or mathematics related fields and office administration – and tasks such as research and translating or summarising documents – may be more exposed to AI displacement, the effect may be more complex.

“Automation can reduce employment, but it can also complement other tasks that require humans, making them more productive, creating new tasks and driving demand,” he says. “And if it increases real incomes, and money gets spent – especially on things humans produce – demand for labour in those areas may grow.”

items.title: Farmers warned to pay up or potentially lose drivers licences
paras: Colin Fenton (right) says he will not cave to pressure to pay his fine. ( Supplied: Colin Fenton )
Victorian drivers can lose their licence if they do not pay a fine, even if the offence is not driving-related.
Many farmers in the path of VNI West have been fined for refusing access to their land.
The Coalition says it will scrap VNI West and waive associated fines if it wins the state election.
Farmers fined for fighting the controversial VNI West transmission line are being warned they face penalties including no longer being able to drive.
If you do not pay a fine in Victoria, the state government can take away your drivers licence, deregister your vehicle, take money from your bank account or sell your land or other assets.
These penalties are now confronting farmers in Victoria's north-west who have been fined for denying VNI West developers access to their land and are refusing to pay up.
The threat of being put off the road was met with incredulity and outrage among farmers, given the fines they received had no connection to driving offences.
Many farmers have locked the gate to VNI West transmission line builders, despite threats of fines and further penalties. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton )
In 2024, he learned the VNI West transmission line would cut through his farm.
Since then, he has fought against the project, which he says would disrupt his farming operations and devalue his property.
He has refused to grant project planners access to his land, and in August this year was one of 12 farmers fined $814 each for doing so.
He now faces losing his drivers licence and having his vehicles deregistered.
Farmers have received this information on their infringement notices, describing the penalties they face if they do not pay up. ( Supplied: Trent Carter )
"I was appalled due to the fact they've connected the fine to road traffic offences," he said.
Mr Fenton said despite the threat of losing his licence, he would not be paying the fine, and would risk driving while unlicensed.

"We live out of town and there is no public transport and we need our drivers licences to run our farms, to get provisions, and in my case I've got a very sick wife and we take regular trips to Bendigo, an hour and a half away," he said.
"I find it pretty intolerable — are we living in a communistic country, or where are we living?"
Farmers have held numerous rallies against VNI West, which they do not want built across their land. ( ABC News: Tamara Clark )
Mark Woods is a specialist in criminal law and past president of the Law Institute of Victoria.
He said driving-related penalties for unpaid fines disproportionately punished rural and regional Victorians.
"It's particularly concerning, because whether you have your licence suspended has nothing to do with where you live," he said.
"So if you're in a regional area with no access to public transport … you can lose your ability to travel about, notwithstanding that you might be the safest driver in the state.

'It's interesting that it's state election time, and therefore if people are concerned about the law, they ought to find out what candidates are going to do it about it, particularly for people in regional Victoria."
Mark Woods says driving-related penalties affect regional Victorians more than their urban counterparts. ( Supplied: Mark Woods )
Mr Woods said the current penalty structure had been in place since 2014.

"In 2014 there was a law passed called the Fines Reform Act, and that created an agency called Fines Victoria, and there's a director of Fines Victoria who has a whole lot of powers to do things to you if you don't pay your fines," he said.

"Fines Victoria can direct VicRoads to suspend your licence or suspend the registration of the car, direct the sheriff to go out and find property that you own that can be sold to pay the fine, or seize control of your land and have that sold for the purposes of paying the fine."
Mr Woods said a term of imprisonment was also possible under the legislation, although there had been a moratorium on that since 2024.
Mr Fenton is hinging his hopes on a change of government on November 28.
While Labor is firmly committed to VNI West, the Coalition and One Nation have vowed to scrap it and waive the fines of those who have resisted it.
"There's about a 90 per cent chance there's going to be a change of government and fortunately now all parties other than Labor and the Greens have said things will be quashed," Mr Fenton said.
Colin Fenton has locked his gate to VNI West builders, and has been fined for doing so. ( Supplied: The Kerang Shebang )
A Labor spokesperson said anyone who believed an infringement notice was issued in error or had exceptional circumstances could seek an internal review.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice and Community Safety, in which Fines Victoria sits, said people who had received fines had options.

"Fines Victoria provides a range of options for people to deal with their fines — people can seek a review of their fine or apply for the Work and Development Permit Scheme or other specialist schemes," they said.
The spokesperson said licence suspension would only come after the issuing of the original fine, a penalty reminder notice, and a notice of final demand.

items.title: Calls to fund Indigenous disaster response ahead of more flooding
paras: The disaster preparedness scorecard highlights gaps in government funding. ( ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick )
Aboriginal organisations are not given the resources they need to prepare for natural disasters, researchers say.
Central Australia is entering another wet season but councils are struggling to access recovery funding after widespread flooding earlier this year.
Researchers are calling for $20 million in existing federal disaster preparedness funds to be set aside for Indigenous organisations.
Aboriginal communities across Central Australia could face another major flood before fully recovering from the last, prompting calls for greater investment in Indigenous-led disaster preparedness.
Months after widespread flooding damaged roads and isolated remote communities in February and March, some regional councils are still struggling to access disaster recovery funding.
Bhiamie Williamson says natural disasters disproportionately effect first nations people. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn )
Monash University professor Bhiamie Williamson said communities were increasingly being forced to prepare for new emergencies while recovering from previous disasters.
"These events are happening with such frequency and ferocity now that communities have to prepare for the next one at the same time as they're recovering from the previous one," he said.
Professor Williamson leads the National Indigenous Disaster Resilience Research Program, which released its latest national disaster preparedness scorecard in October.
The report found 50 of Australia's 63 declared natural disasters over the preceding year disproportionately affected First Nations communities.
Floodwater from the Todd River covered the Undoolya Road crossing in Alice Springs in March. ( Victoria Ellis )
It also identified significant gaps in government investment, partnerships and reporting on Indigenous disaster preparedness.
Professor Williamson said his research showed Aboriginal people accounted for 68 per cent of those affected by flooding in the Northern Territory earlier this year.
He said remote Aboriginal organisations were often best placed to respond when emergencies struck, particularly where distance limited access to emergency services.
"They're best placed to provide that relief and support for communities and yet they're not funded to do so and there's no partnerships that support them to play that active role," he said.
The scorecard identified the Northern Territory as an exception in having established formal partnerships with major Aboriginal land councils.
However, Professor Williamson said investment in community-controlled organisations remained inadequate, while gaps in government reporting made progress difficult to measure.
First Nations Response founder and CEO Coral Lever said Aboriginal organisations frequently carried the burden of emergency relief without having adequate resources.
Her Sydney-based grassroots organisation began providing food relief during the COVID-19 pandemic. It has since expanded into disaster response assistance and advocacy.
Coral Lever says Aboriginal-led organisations need more funding to help communities prepare for disasters. ( Supplied: First Nations Response. )
"First Nations Response is doing all of this work entirely without support or funding," she said.
Ms Lever said the lack of funding limited her organisation's ability to respond and placed significant pressure on its workers.
Coral Lever says Aboriginal organisations, such as ranger groups, are often best placed to respond to disasters in remote communities. ( Supplied: Monash University )
She said remote communities could benefit from having essential supplies, food storage and locally trained emergency personnel established before flooding cut off road access.
"If we're funded and resourced to be able to do this work long before a disaster strikes, it means the resilience level in the community is going to be so much stronger," she said.
Professor Williamson is calling for $20 million from the existing federal Disaster Ready Fund to be reserved for Indigenous-led preparedness projects.
He said the money should be used to support Aboriginal organisations before disasters occurred, rather than diverted from essential services during emergencies.
The concerns follow ABC reporting in October that three Central Australian councils had experienced difficulties accessing disaster recovery funding.
Storms in October caused widespread damage in Alice Springs. ( ABC Alice Springs: Charles Geary )
The federal emergency management minister acknowledged delays and said a national taskforce was examining the arrangements.
The NT government also acknowledged that national funding requirements were difficult for some councils and said it was working with the Commonwealth on reforms.
Professor Williamson said more enduring partnerships and investment were needed to prevent Aboriginal communities being left behind.
"These are very serious issues that require a different way of investing and different way of partnering that's not ad hoc, that is ongoing, that's systemic," he said.

items.title: Reserve Bank issues Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations
paras: The Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 were superseded by the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, which were issued on January 13, 2026 , and became effective from October 01, 2026. The new regulations are principle based; intended to promote ease of doing business, especially for small exporters and importers; and empower Authorised Dealers to provide quicker and more efficient service to their customers. Based on subsequent feedback received from stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has issued Amendment Regulations to Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 that were notified on November 02, 2026 , and came into effect, retrospectively, from October 01, 2026 . In this regard, to facilitate better understanding of the new trade regulations by the exporters/importers and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has placed a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 on its website. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1531

items.title: RBI imposes monetary penalty on Fusion Finance Limited
paras: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 17, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹7.50 lakh (Rupees Seven Lakh Fifty Thousand only) on Fusion Finance Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of directions issued by RBI on ‘Know Your Customer (KYC)’ and ‘Internal Ombudsman’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under section 58G(1)(b) read with section 58B(5)(aa) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its financial position as on March 31, 2026. Based on the supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for failure to comply with the RBI directions. After considering the company's reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: The company failed to obtain PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form 60 from customers, while establishing an account-based relationship with those customers; and, The company failed to escalate the partly or wholly rejected complaints to the Internal Ombudsman for a final decision within the prescribed time. This action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of this monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1537

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "C-295 facility represents work culture of New India," says PM Modi as he and Spanish PM inaugurate facility
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Vadodara (Gujarat) [ India ], October 28 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday inaugurated the TATA- Airbus aircraft assembly facility complex in Vadodara. The facility will manufacture C-295 aircraft at the TATA Advanced Systems Limited campus. PM Modi said that the C-295 facility represents the work culture of a new India . "Recently, we lost the country's great son Ratan Tata ji. If he had been among us today, he would have been happy, but wherever his soul is, he would be happy. This C-295 aircraft factory reflects the new work culture of New India ... When I was the Gujarat CM, it was decided to set up a factory in Vadodara to build train coaches. The factory was also prepared for production within a record time. Today, we are exporting the metro coaches manufactured in that factory to other countries. I am confident that in the future, the aircraft made in this factory will also be exported to other countries," PM Modi said. "Today the defence manufacturing ecosystem in India is touching new heights. If we had not taken concrete steps 10 years ago, it would have been impossible to reach this level today. At that time, no one could even imagine that there could be such large-scale defence manufacturing in India . But we decided to walk on the new path, set a new goal for ourselves. And today the result is before us," PM Modi added. The Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez underlined the importance of the new industrial site. Sanchez said, "Today we are not only officially inaugurating a cutting-edge industrial facility. Today we're also witnessing how an extraordinary project between two emblematic companies becomes a reality. Prime Minister Modi, this is another triumph of your vision. Your vision is to turn India into an industrial powerhouse and a magnet for investment and business. This partnership between Airbus and Tata will contribute to the progress of the India n aerospace industry and will open new doors for the arrival of other European companies." " Tata is probably the best exponent of India n industrial strength. Its products and services are present in virtually every country on the planet. Tata is a giant among giants. As for Airbus , it embodies the very essence of a united Europe. Committed to technological innovation and the creation of jobs and prosperity. For my country, for Spain , being an integral part of the Airbus consortium, defending the values it represents. Values on which the very idea of Europe is based on cooperation, modernity and progress," Sanchez added. During the inauguration of the TATA Aircraft Complex for manufacturing C-295 aircraft, Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran announced the facility's goals. "The final aircraft assembly complex for the first aircraft to be delivered is being set up here. I must commit to our Prime Minister that exactly two years from now we will deliver the first indigenously manufactured aircraft and we will request and we'll work with your office to block the date so that you can come and inaugurate the facility and receive the first product. The first 200 engineers from Tata Group are already in Spain going through the training that is required, and we have worked with 40 SME companies and we will be adding more companies to build the entire localisation that is required for the product," he said. This collaboration between Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL) and Airbus Spain will mark India 's first private sector final assembly line (FAL) for military aircraft, boosting the nation's aerospace capabilities. The plant, located at TASL's Vadodara campus, is part of India 's Rs 2.5 billion deal signed in 2021 to acquire 56 C-295 military transport aircraft from Airbus . Under the agreement, Airbus will deliver 16 aircraft directly from Spain , while the remaining 40 will be manufactured in India by TASL. This project will create a comprehensive ecosystem for aircraft development, covering assembly, testing, certification, and maintenance throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft. Major India n defence players like Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) and Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL), along with smaller enterprises, are also contributing to this project. The C-295 aircraft will strengthen India 's Air Force fleet with a modern and more reliable transport solution. Earlier in the day, PM Modi and Sanchez participated in a roadshow in Vadodara as they headed to inaugurate Tata Advanced Systems Ltd's facility. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
paras: CREDENTIAL COMPROMISE AT SCALE Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced. Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.

25 ... ... ... Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g. OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
The most concerning of the findings was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging, and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

items.title: Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Where does mathematics go from here? 2011 The Washington Post If the past year was the “ mathpocalypse ”, a claim that AI has helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis is its most stunning horseman yet. Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic says he has used AI to solve this problem, which has sat at the heart of mathematics for nearly 200 years. This is not just the latest in the series of famed mathematics problems to fall to AI , but could be the biggest mathematical result of the century. Accordingly, mathematicians have received the news with a combination of exhilaration, bewilderment and caution.

“If true, it would, in my opinion. be the greatest achievement yet by AI, and one of the greatest proofs in the history of mathematics,” says Thomas Bloom at the University of Manchester in the UK. “The Riemann hypothesis has represented a major barrier in our current understanding of the way numbers behave – if the AI proof has correctly solved it, this would represent a huge leap in what we know.”

Rainer Dietmann at Royal Holloway University of London in the UK is similarly in awe. “If it turns out to be correct, this is not only huge, it’s the biggest result in pure mathematics ever…It’s like having found the Holy Grail,” he says.

Dating back to the 1800s, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers. Because they cannot be factored into any smaller whole numbers, primes are like the atoms of numbers – they are the simplest units out of which any other number can be made. However, predicting when a prime will show up in a list of numbers is notoriously difficult. In 1859, Bernhard Reimann hypothesised a formula that would stunningly reduce that difficulty, but didn’t finish a proof before he died. Mathematicians have been trying to wrangle it ever since. After years of approximate results, including an AI-generated proof released by Open AI in October, Alpöge’s work may have finally confirmed Reimann’s centuries’ old intuition.

“It has captured the imagination, presumably because it is about something that we can all understand – the prime numbers – and because it has resisted the efforts of so many for so long. And it is important to mathematicians because it is so useful for other problems: a lot of theorems begin, “Assume the Riemann hypothesis…,” says Chris Daw at the University of Reading in the UK.

The new proof has not been formally reviewed by other mathematicians, which would be required for publication in an academic journal, and Alpöge has not released the full proof, which he described in a public statement as being over 250,000 pages long. Instead, he has released the version of the proof that has been adapted for verification in the proof-checking software Lean , which is 17 million lines long. Anthropic and Alpöge did not respond to New Scientist ’s request for comment.

Michael Levitin at the University of Reading in the UK says hundreds of thousands of pages of Lean output will not be easily checked. “In proportion to the magnitude of this claim, we should be appropriately sceptical,” says Bloom. “Even after the Lean formalisation has been independently checked, it remains possible that the AI might be taking advantage of some subtle undiscovered bug in the code. I’d feel more confident once we have a combination of the Lean compiling correctly, with no bugs found, and also human experts [having] had a chance to discuss the ‘big picture’ of the proof and whether it seems plausible.”

“Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to understand the proof themselves. And that will of course take time, since we only move at biological speeds,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas, Austin. It is here that this new result, with its prospect of incredible historical significance, exemplifies the trouble mathematicians have had with AI over the past year, as it has been used to check one problem after another off their most coveted list of open questions.

Put simply, AI-assisted work benefits tremendously from prior work by human mathematicians, yet its end result is not immediately understandable to them. Coming to terms with the new proof will almost certainly take a long time, and it brings to the fore big questions about the future of mathematics. “Pretty much every mathematician will need time to process this. If AI can do this, what can it not do – in mathematics, at least?” says Daw. Many mathematicians already feel a sense of grief and anguish over how quickly AI tools have been solving problems that would have previously consumed a human mathematician’s whole career, and Dietmann says this new proof could have a similarly negative effect.

“What looked impossible one year ago has become reality. Many other problems in mathematics, computer science and related fields will fall as well, and it will become increasingly difficult for humans even to follow and understand,” he says. “While this progress is tremendous, it will massively amplify the despair by many in the mathematical community.”

Some mathematicians are more optimistic. “This is a very exciting time for pure mathematicians, and we are needed more than ever,” says Alex Bartel at Glasgow University. “AI is capable of spitting out proofs at a much faster pace than we are used to, but our task remains that of properly understanding what is going … and that work is as fulfilling as ever, but there is now a lot more of it. The announcement of a very long proof of the Riemann Hypothesis only reinforces my view.”

Mere hours after Alpöge’s announcement, president of the American Mathematical Society Ravi Vakil wrote in a blog post that mathematician Alessandro Masullo has also put forward a proof of a generalised version of the Riemann hypothesis . This proof was completed without the use of AI, and it is 940 pages long. It has also not yet been checked by other mathematicians nor confirmed using Lean.

This day will be remembered as a shocking one, and the aftershocks may continue. “I can only compare this achievement to the aliens with a vastly superior intelligence coming to the Earth and explaining to us all the sacred mysteries we ever dreamed of,” says Alexei Skorobogatov at Imperial College London. “Humanity managed to create an amazingly powerful, yet completely alien form of intelligence. The only event in history I can compare it to is the discovery of a nuclear bomb. Hopefully, AI will be put to better use!”

items.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
paras: A state’s rights Trump FCC declares California isn’t allowed to enforce phone service rules FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

4 ... ... ... AT&T's stand at Mobile World Congress on February 27, 2023, in Barcelona, Spain. Credit: Getty Images | Joan Cros Garcia-Corbis AT&T's stand at Mobile World Congress on February 27, 2023, in Barcelona, Spain. Credit: Getty Images | Joan Cros Garcia-Corbis Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

items.title: Daniil Medvedev Cruises Into Nitto ATP Finals Semi-Finals With Win Over Tiafoe
paras: Daniil Medvedev is into the semi-finals at the Nitto ATP Finals after a 6-3 6-4 win over Frances Tiafoe in Turin. The former champion is into the final four in Turin after he defeated Tiafoe in straight sets in what was a comfortable victory for the fourth seed.

It means that Tiafoe’s season is now over as he qualified for the first Nitto ATP Finals tournament of his career but fell short of the final four. World number one Alexander Zverev now awaits in the final four on Saturday.

It was a fast start from both players in what was a crucial match and essentially a ‘quarter-final’ with both players serving incredibly well. The forehand was in particular a crucial shot in this match as both players were effective in this match with that specific shot.

items.title: “Not that hungry just because I’m super tired”: Medvedev, drained but still fighting in Turin
paras: After beating Tiafoe 6-3, 6-4 to reach the ATP Finals semi-finals, the No. 4 seed says a packed end of season “drains you”, ties his return to the top level to consistency and would be happy to go back to Dubai and Doha.

Daniil Medvedev admits he is running on empty, but does not see it as a reason to stop winning. Asked on Friday in Turin how hungry he still is for the big titles, after beating Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 6-4 to reach the semi-finals of the ATP Finals, the world No.

On Saturday, he faces Alexander Zverev , who topped Group McEnroe unbeaten . “Today and this tournament, not that hungry, just because I’m super tired. But again, I’m fighting, I’m working hard, and that I’m tired doesn’t mean that I cannot win,” he said.
items.impact: His year also included a final at Indian Wells, where he beat Carlos Alcaraz in the semi-finals before losing to Jannik Sinner.

items.title: Daniil Medvedev claims he knows exactly what to expect from his ATP Finals semi-final vs Alexander Zverev
paras: In what was effectively an unofficial quarter-final match of this year’s ATP Finals, it was Daniil Medvedev who emerged victorious, beating Frances Tiafoe in straight sets earlier tonight. Before the match began, it was already confirmed that the winner would secure qualification from the group, whilst the loser would be out.

And, it was noted that whoever did emerge victorious would get the pleasure of facing Alexander Zverev in the semi-finals, the two-time champion of this tournament, and year-end world number one for 2026. We are now guaranteed to enjoy a generational showdown between two major champions for a spot in Sunday’s final.

Daniil Medvedev spoke whilst still on court afterwards, and looked ahead to what he expects from their match. Chatting with Tennis Channel, he began with an overview of his impressive win over Tiafoe.

items.title: ATP Finals Semifinal Predictions Including Carlos Alcaraz vs Ben Shelton
paras: In one, the in-form Carlos Alcaraz will take on would-be challenger Ben Shelton, whilst in the other, world #1 Alexander Zverev faces off against Daniil Medvedev.
It should be an entertaining day of tennis under the roof at the Palasport Olimpico, but who will book their place in Sunday’s showpiece final?

Their rivalry essentially has shown that Shelton can compete with Alcaraz , but he can’t really beat him – at least not if the Spaniard is firing on all cylinders. The American will be able to take some confidence from his victory in the quarterfinals at the US Open, but Alcaraz was clearly short of a gallop in New York having missed so much tennis in the lead-in . When he was match-sharp again, the rivalry resumed its previous pattern in the ATP Paris Masters final.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
